title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about delivering a presentation well, across the formats you meet at university. You already know what a presentation is; here you build the skills that make one land. By the end you will be able to adapt your approach to a format and brief, structure and design a presentation that supports your delivery, and spot and correct the errors that weaken it.

Presentations are assessed in almost every subject, and the same skills carry into interviews and professional life. Delivering well is not about confidence alone. It rests on preparation that fits the task, a structure the audience can follow, and the judgement to avoid the common pitfalls.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: adapt how you prepare and deliver a presentation to suit its format and assessment brief
structure and design a presentation so that it supports clear delivery
identify and correct common delivery errors that weaken a presentation.

title: In real academic practice
body: Presentations run through your degree and beyond it. Every assessed talk, poster, group pitch and seminar presentation draws on the same skills: reading the task, building a structure, and delivering without the common errors. Build them now and they carry into interviews, meetings and the professional presentations your working life will ask of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, choosing your approach for the format: reading the brief so your preparation fits. Second, structuring and designing for delivery: building a structure and visual aids that carry the audience. Third, avoiding common delivery errors: spotting and correcting what undoes a presentation. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people and scenarios to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name or situation you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You already know what a presentation is and roughly how one is built. This course is about delivering one well, and that work starts before you speak. A presentation that succeeds in one format can fall flat in another. This lesson is about reading the format and the brief, so your preparation fits the task in front of you.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are moving from giving a presentation to giving the right presentation for the occasion. You are expected to look past a single default style and ask what this particular format and brief reward, then prepare accordingly.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: match a presentation format to what its assessment brief is really testing
adapt your preparation to the demands of a given format
select the format features that matter most for a presentation in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Presentations come in several formats, and each is assessed differently. An individual talk, a poster, a group presentation, a professional pitch and an interview presentation all share a core skill, but each rewards something particular. A poster rewards clear visual design; a group presentation rewards coordination; an interview presentation rewards concision under pressure.

Delivering well starts with reading the brief and the marking criteria closely. They tell you what the format is really testing, so you can prepare for that rather than for a presentation in general. Matching your approach to the format is the first move of an effective presenter.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a presentation you have given, or one coming up. What format was it, and did you prepare for that format, or present the way you usually do? What is one thing you would change?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Delivering a presentation well begins before you speak, with reading the format and the brief. Different formats reward different things, so the first move is to ask what this one is testing and prepare for that. You can now match a format to what its brief rewards and adapt your preparation to fit. The next lesson builds the structure and visual aids that carry a delivery.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you matched your approach to the format. This lesson is about building the presentation itself so that it supports you when you deliver it. A clear structure and well-judged visual aids do a lot of the work: they carry the audience through your argument and leave you free to present, rather than to rescue a muddle.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are expected to do more than put slides in an order. The aim is to structure a presentation so that each part has a job, and to design visual aids that support your argument instead of competing with it. These are deliberate choices, not defaults.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: adapt the structure of a presentation to its format and audience so the introduction, main body and conclusion support delivery
design visual aids that support your argument rather than compete with it
apply a supporting structure to a presentation in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A presentation that delivers well has a structure the audience can follow. An introduction tells them what to expect and why it matters. A main body develops the argument in a clear order, one point leading to the next. A conclusion draws the threads together and leaves a single, memorable message. This shape is set at the planning stage, and refined as you rehearse.

Visual aids are there to support that structure, not to replace it. The presentation is about your argument and how you deliver it, so slides should prompt and illustrate, not carry dense text you read aloud. A good visual aid makes a point land faster than words alone; a poor one splits the audience's attention between you and the screen.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last presentation you built. Did a structure lead it, or did the slides? What is one change to the structure or the visual aids that would help your audience follow you?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A presentation delivers well when a clear structure leads it and the visual aids serve that structure. An introduction, an ordered main body and a conclusion give the audience a path to follow, and slides that prompt rather than script keep their attention on you. You can now build a supporting structure and design visual aids that back your argument. The final lesson looks at the errors that undo good preparation.

title: Orientation
body: You have matched your approach to the format and built a structure that supports delivery. This lesson is about the things that still go wrong on the day. Many presentations are undone not by weak content but by a handful of common errors. Knowing them, and how to correct them, protects the work you have put in.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are expected to do more than avoid obvious mistakes. The aim is to tell a genuine error apart from a reasonable delivery choice, and to know the correction for each, so you can check your own presentation before you give it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: analyse how a common delivery error would weaken a presentation for a given audience
compare a delivery error with an effective delivery choice for a given format
correct a common error in a presentation in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Most presentation errors fall into a few familiar groups. Reading from the slides word for word turns a talk into a recital and loses the audience. Overrunning the time shows a plan that was never rehearsed. Overloading slides with text splits attention between you and the screen. Rushing, mumbling or avoiding eye contact all weaken the connection with the audience, however strong the content.

What these have in common is that each is fixable before the day. The correction is rarely more work; it is usually less. Fewer words on a slide, a rehearsal to time, a pause instead of a rush. Spotting the error is most of the cure, which is why knowing the common ones is worth your time.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about presentations you have seen, including your own. Which of these common errors do you notice most often? Which one are you most likely to make, and what is the fix you would reach for?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Good content can still be undone by a few common errors: reading the slides, overrunning, overloaded slides, and losing the audience. Each one is fixable before the day, and spotting it is most of the cure. You can now identify these errors, tell them apart from sound delivery choices, and correct them. With a fitting approach, a supporting structure and the errors in check, you are ready to deliver well.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Delivering a presentation well is no longer a matter of nerve alone: it is a set of choices you can make on purpose. You can read a format and its brief and adapt your preparation to fit. You can build a structure, with an introduction, an ordered body and a clear conclusion, and design visual aids that support it. And you can spot the common errors that undo a presentation, and correct them before the day. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, delivering well is something you practise in every presentation you give. Each time you read a brief, build a structure, or cut a slide to a prompt, these skills are at work. They travel beyond your degree too: interviews, pitches and workplace briefings all reward the presenter who prepares for the task and avoids the common errors.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced presenting course takes you into presenting with authority and collaborating, including group work, the roles people take, and handling disagreement. Going wider: the same skills support Academic Writing, where structure and argument matter, and Reflective Practice, where you review how a delivery went and improve it.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four common presentation formats, and what each one is really assessing.
instruction: Select each card to see what the format rewards. Work through all four.

_items.title: Individual talk
_items.subtitle: You, on your own
_items.text: A solo talk tests your own command of the material and your ability to hold an audience without anyone to share the load. Prepare to carry every part yourself.

_items.title: Poster
_items.subtitle: Design does the talking
_items.text: A poster is read as much as heard. It rewards a clear visual layout and a sharp headline message, with you on hand to answer questions rather than narrate every point.

_items.title: Group presentation
_items.subtitle: Shared delivery
_items.text: A group format tests coordination as well as content: smooth handovers, a consistent line, and each member clearly contributing. Rehearse the joins, not only your own section.

_items.title: Interview or practice-based
_items.subtitle: Concise, to a purpose
_items.text: A pitch at interview or in a professional setting rewards concision and relevance. Read what the panel or client needs, and cut anything that does not serve it.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students are set the same task: a ten-minute presentation assessed against a marking brief.

{{learner-a}} prepares the way they always do: a full set of slides, every point written out, and a plan to read through them. The content is sound, but {{learner-a}} has not looked at what the brief rewards or how long the slot really is. On the day the talk overruns, the slides are dense, and the marker sees preparation but little judgement. This is a default approach applied to every format.

{{learner-b}} starts with the brief and the criteria. The format is a short individual talk that rewards a clear argument and good timing, so {{learner-b}} cuts to three points, builds slides that prompt rather than script, and rehearses to time. The content is no deeper, but it fits the format, and the delivery lands. This is adapting to the task.

Both students knew their material. Only {{learner-b}} read the format and the brief, and prepared for the presentation actually being asked for.

title: Match your approach to the format
body: These habits turn a brief into a plan that fits. Try them on your next presentation.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I read the brief and marking criteria before planning anything?
Do I know which format this is, and what it mainly rewards?
Have I checked the time limit and planned my content to fit it?
Have I designed slides or visual aids to suit this format, not my usual one?
Have I identified the one or two things this format is really testing?
Have I rehearsed in the conditions the format sets, such as to time or as a group?

title: Formative check: formats and briefs
displayTitle: A poster, a group talk and an interview pitch are all presentations. Why does each need a different approach?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does each presentation format need a different approach?

_items.text: Each format rewards something particular, so the brief tests different skills.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reading what a format rewards is how you match your approach to it.

_items.text: Longer formats are always worth more marks than shorter ones.
_items.feedback: Length does not set the marks; what the format tests does.

_items.text: Posters are easier than talks, so they need less preparation.
_items.feedback: A poster is not easier; it simply rewards different things, such as visual design.

_items.text: The format makes no real difference once the content is strong.
_items.feedback: The format changes what counts as strong; the same content can land or fail.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Each format rewards something particular, so you prepare for what its brief is testing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what each format is really assessing, rather than its length or difficulty.
_incorrect.final: Each format rewards something particular, so the brief tests different skills. Length, difficulty and content alone do not explain the difference.

title: Formative check: adapting preparation
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that the first did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do that the first did not?

_items.text: Read the brief and format, then adapted the preparation to fit them.
_items.feedback: Yes. Adapting preparation to the format is what made the difference.

_items.text: Prepared more slides and wrote out every point.
_items.feedback: More slides and full text is the first student's default approach.

_items.text: Chose a longer time slot for the talk.
_items.feedback: The slot was the same; the difference was preparing to fit it.

_items.text: Used the same approach they always use.
_items.feedback: Using the same default is exactly what the first student did.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student read the brief and format and adapted their preparation to fit.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student did differently with the brief and the format.
_incorrect.final: The second student read the brief and format and adapted their preparation. More slides, a longer slot or a default approach are not what made the difference.

title: Formative check: choosing for the format
displayTitle: You are preparing a presentation in {{context}}. Which approach best fits delivering well for its format?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach best fits delivering well for the format?

_items.text: Check what the brief rewards and shape your preparation around it.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, letting the brief shape your preparation is the move this lesson teaches.

_items.text: Prepare the same way regardless of the format or brief.
_items.feedback: A single default ignores what this particular format rewards.

_items.text: Add as many slides as possible to show the depth of your work.
_items.feedback: Depth of slides is not what a format tests; fit to the brief is.

_items.text: Decide the format matters less than how much you know.
_items.feedback: Knowing the material is not enough if the delivery does not fit the format.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you shape your preparation around what the brief rewards.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that lets the brief and format guide your preparation.
_incorrect.final: Delivering well in {{context}} means checking what the brief rewards and preparing for that, not applying a default or piling on slides.

title: Explore the concept
body: The parts of a presentation that carries an audience, and the job each one does.
instruction: Step through each stage to see the job it does.

_items.title: Set the scene
_items.body: Tell the audience what the presentation covers, why it matters, and the route you will take. A clear opening earns their attention and shows them how to follow you.

_items.title: Develop the argument
_items.body: Take one point at a time, in an order where each leads to the next. Signpost the moves so the audience always knows where they are. This is where the substance sits.

_items.title: Land the message
_items.body: Draw the threads together and leave one clear message the audience will remember. Do not introduce new material here; the job is to close, not to open.

_items.title: Let visual aids support
_items.body: At every stage, visual aids should prompt and illustrate rather than carry the talk. If a slide could be read without you, it is doing your job rather than supporting it.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students present on the same topic, with the same findings to share.

{{learner-a}} builds the slides first and lets them set the order. Each slide is full of text, and the talk becomes a reading of the screen. The talk has no clear opening or close, so the audience is unsure what the main point is, and the visual aids pull their eyes away from {{learner-a}} rather than supporting the argument. The material is all there, but it does not land.

{{learner-b}} plans the structure first: an introduction that frames the question, a main body of three ordered points, and a conclusion with one clear message. Only then do the slides follow, each one a prompt or an image that supports a point. The audience can follow the argument, and the visual aids help it along. The delivery feels in control.

Both had the same findings. Only {{learner-b}} let a structure lead and made the visual aids serve it.

title: Build for delivery
body: These checks keep a structure and its visual aids working for you. Try them on your next build.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Does my introduction say what the presentation covers and why it matters?
Does the main body take one point at a time, in a clear order?
Have I signposted the moves so the audience knows where they are?
Does my conclusion leave one memorable message, with nothing new added?
Does each visual aid support a point rather than carry dense text?
Could any slide be read without me? If so, have I cut it to a prompt?

title: Formative check: a structure that supports delivery
displayTitle: You want your audience to follow your argument from start to finish. Which structure best supports that?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which structure best supports an audience following your argument?

_items.text: An introduction, an ordered main body, and a conclusion with one clear message.
_items.feedback: Yes. That shape gives the audience a path to follow.

_items.text: As many slides as the time allows, in any order.
_items.feedback: A pile of slides in no order is not a structure.

_items.text: A single long section, so you do not lose your place.
_items.feedback: One long section gives the audience nothing to follow.

_items.text: A detailed script on the slides that you read out.
_items.feedback: A script on the slides is the problem this lesson warns against.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An introduction, an ordered body and a clear conclusion carry the audience.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that gives the audience a clear path to follow.
_incorrect.final: A supporting structure has an introduction, an ordered main body and a conclusion with one message. A pile of slides, one long block or an on-screen script do not.

title: Formative check: visual aids that support
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second student's visual aids work better than the first student's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second student's visual aids work better?

_items.text: They supported each point as prompts or images, rather than carrying dense text.
_items.feedback: Yes. Visual aids that prompt keep the audience's attention on the speaker.

_items.text: They used brighter colours and more animation.
_items.feedback: Colour and animation are not what made the difference here.

_items.text: There were more slides, so the audience saw more.
_items.feedback: More slides do not help; it is how they support each point that matters.

_items.text: They were written out in full so the student could read them.
_items.feedback: Full text on slides is the first student's error, not the fix.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The visual aids supported each point as prompts, rather than carrying the talk.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the visual aids were doing, not how they looked.
_incorrect.final: The second student's visual aids worked because they prompted and supported each point. Colour, more slides or full text are not what made them effective.

title: Formative check: applying a structure
displayTitle: You are structuring a presentation in {{context}}. Which move best supports your delivery?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move best supports your delivery?

_items.text: Plan the introduction, ordered body and conclusion first, then let the slides follow.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, letting a structure lead is what supports the delivery.

_items.text: Build the slides first and present in whatever order they fall.
_items.feedback: Letting the slides set the order is the error the worked example showed.

_items.text: Put the full argument on the slides so you do not have to remember it.
_items.feedback: A full argument on the slides turns the talk into a reading.

_items.text: Leave the structure loose so you can improvise on the day.
_items.feedback: A loose structure gives the audience no path to follow.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, you plan the structure first and let the slides follow.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where a structure leads and the slides serve it.
_incorrect.final: A structure that supports delivery is planned first, with the slides following. Building slides first, scripting them, or leaving the structure loose all weaken the delivery.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four errors that weaken a presentation, and the correction for each.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal the error and how to correct it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Reading from the slides
_items.body: Reading your slides word for word turns delivery into a recital and breaks the connection with the audience. The fix: cut slides to prompts and keywords, and talk to the audience rather than to the screen.

_items.title: Overrunning the time
_items.body: Running over shows a plan that was not rehearsed, and it often means the conclusion is rushed or cut. The fix: rehearse to time, and plan what to drop if you are running late, so the ending still lands.

_items.title: Overloaded slides
_items.body: Dense slides make the audience read instead of listen, and split their attention from you. The fix: one idea per slide, few words, and an image or diagram where it makes a point land faster than text.

_items.title: Losing the audience
_items.body: Rushing, mumbling, or fixing your eyes on your notes all weaken the connection, however good the content. The fix: slow down, pause between points, and look up at the audience to bring them with you.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students give the same presentation to the same seminar group.

{{learner-a}} has strong material but faces the screen and reads each slide aloud. The slides are full of text, the talk runs three minutes over, and the conclusion is rushed to make up time. The group follows the slides, not the speaker, and the main point is lost in the overrun. The content deserved better than its delivery.

{{learner-b}} gives the same content but has checked it against the common errors. The slides are cut to prompts, so the talk is to the audience, not the screen. It has been rehearsed to time, with a point planned to drop if needed, so the conclusion lands cleanly. The group follows the argument, and the message stays with them.

The material was identical. Only {{learner-b}} corrected the errors that would otherwise have undone it.

title: Check before you present
body: Run through these before the day to catch the common errors in your own presentation.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Have I cut my slides to prompts, so I am not reading them aloud?
Have I rehearsed to time, and planned what to drop if I run late?
Does each slide carry one idea, in few words, rather than dense text?
Have I practised looking up at the audience rather than at my notes?
Do I pause between points instead of rushing through them?
Have I checked my presentation against the common errors before the day?

title: Formative check: spotting an error
displayTitle: A classmate is presenting to an audience new to the topic. Which choice would most weaken how that audience follows the talk?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which choice would most weaken how a new audience follows the talk?

_items.text: Reading the slides word for word instead of talking to the audience.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reading the slides is one of the most common delivery errors.

_items.text: Rehearsing the talk to time before the day.
_items.feedback: Rehearsing to time is a correction, not an error.

_items.text: Using one clear image to make a point land.
_items.feedback: A clear image that supports a point is good practice.

_items.text: Leaving a pause between the main points.
_items.feedback: A pause between points helps the audience; it is not an error.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading the slides word for word is a common error that loses the audience.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Three of these are sound delivery choices; look for the one that weakens a talk.
_incorrect.final: Reading the slides word for word is the error. Rehearsing to time, using a clear image and pausing between points are all sound choices.

title: Formative check: error or effective choice
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that corrected the errors?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do that corrected the errors?

_items.text: Cut the slides to prompts and rehearsed to time, with a point planned to drop.
_items.feedback: Yes. Those corrections let the content land.

_items.text: Added more text to the slides so nothing was forgotten.
_items.feedback: More text on slides is the error, not the fix.

_items.text: Spoke faster to fit all the material in.
_items.feedback: Speaking faster rushes the delivery; it does not correct the overrun.

_items.text: Faced the screen so the slides could be read in full.
_items.feedback: Facing the screen and reading the slides is the first student's error.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Cutting slides to prompts and rehearsing to time corrected the errors.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the corrections that fixed the reading and the overrun.
_incorrect.final: The second student cut the slides to prompts and rehearsed to time, with a point to drop. More text, speaking faster or facing the screen are the errors, not fixes.

title: Formative check: correcting an error
displayTitle: Your presentation in {{context}} overruns every time you rehearse it. Which correction best fits this lesson?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which correction best fits an overrunning presentation?

_items.text: Rehearse to time and plan a point to drop, so the conclusion still lands.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, rehearsing to time with a planned cut protects the ending.

_items.text: Speak faster on the day to fit everything in.
_items.feedback: Speaking faster rushes the delivery and usually loses the audience.

_items.text: Cut the conclusion so the main body fits.
_items.feedback: Cutting the conclusion removes the message the audience should leave with.

_items.text: Add the extra material to the slides and read it quickly.
_items.feedback: Moving material onto the slides and reading it is two errors at once.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, rehearsing to time with a planned cut keeps the conclusion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the correction that protects the conclusion rather than rushing or cutting it.
_incorrect.final: Rehearsing to time and planning a point to drop keeps the conclusion. Speaking faster, cutting the conclusion or reading extra slides all weaken the delivery.

body: A poster, a group talk and an interview pitch assess different things. What should most shape how you prepare for each?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should most shape how you prepare for each format?

_items.text: What that format and its brief are really testing.
_items.feedback: Yes. The format and brief set what you prepare for.

_items.text: How many slides you can prepare in the time.
_items.feedback: Slide count is not what shapes a good preparation.

_items.text: Which format you personally find easiest.
_items.feedback: The format is set by the task, not by preference.

_items.text: How long the session is scheduled to last.
_items.feedback: Length matters, but what the format tests matters more.

_feedback.correct: That's right. What the format and its brief are testing should shape how you prepare.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Review the lesson this question draws on and try again.

body: You are given a presentation brief and marking criteria. What is the first move of an effective presenter?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the first move of an effective presenter?

_items.text: Read them closely to see what the format rewards, then prepare for that.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reading the brief first is the effective presenter's first move.

_items.text: Start building slides straight away to save time.
_items.feedback: Building slides before reading the brief risks preparing the wrong thing.

_items.text: Prepare the way you always do, then adjust at the end.
_items.feedback: A default approach ignores what this brief rewards.

_items.text: Ask for a different format that suits you better.
_items.feedback: The format is set by the task; you adapt to it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The first move is to read the brief and criteria, then prepare for what they reward.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Review the lesson this question draws on and try again.

body: Which structure best supports a clear delivery?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which structure best supports a clear delivery?

_items.text: An introduction, an ordered main body, and a conclusion with one clear message.
_items.feedback: Yes. That shape carries the audience through.

_items.text: One long section, so there are no joins to manage.
_items.feedback: One long section gives the audience nothing to follow.

_items.text: Whatever order the slides happen to fall into.
_items.feedback: Letting the slides set the order is not a structure.

_items.text: A full script on the slides, read out in order.
_items.feedback: A script on the slides turns the talk into a reading.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An introduction, an ordered body and a clear conclusion support delivery.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Review the lesson this question draws on and try again.

body: What is the main job of a visual aid in a presentation?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the main job of a visual aid?

_items.text: To support a point as a prompt or image, not to carry the talk.
_items.feedback: Yes. Visual aids support; they do not replace the speaker.

_items.text: To hold the full text so the speaker can read it aloud.
_items.feedback: Full text to read aloud is the error, not the job.

_items.text: To fill the time with as much detail as possible.
_items.feedback: Filling time with detail splits the audience's attention.

_items.text: To show how much work the speaker has done.
_items.feedback: A visual aid serves the argument, not a display of effort.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A visual aid supports a point as a prompt or image.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Review the lesson this question draws on and try again.

body: Which of these is a common presentation error rather than a sound delivery choice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option is a common presentation error?

_items.text: Reading the slides word for word instead of talking to the audience.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reading the slides is a common error.

_items.text: Pausing between the main points.
_items.feedback: A pause helps the audience; it is a sound choice.

_items.text: Rehearsing the talk to time beforehand.
_items.feedback: Rehearsing to time is a correction, not an error.

_items.text: Using one clear image to make a point.
_items.feedback: A clear image is good practice.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading the slides word for word is the common error here.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Review the lesson this question draws on and try again.

body: Your presentation overruns every time you rehearse it. Which correction best fits?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which correction best fits an overrunning presentation?

_items.text: Rehearse to time and plan a point to drop, so the conclusion still lands.
_items.feedback: Yes. Rehearsing to time with a planned cut protects the ending.

_items.text: Speak faster on the day to fit it all in.
_items.feedback: Speaking faster rushes the delivery and loses the audience.

_items.text: Cut the conclusion so the body fits the slot.
_items.feedback: Cutting the conclusion loses your final message.

_items.text: Move the extra material onto the slides and read it quickly.
_items.feedback: That adds two errors: overloaded slides and reading them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Rehearse to time and plan a point to drop, so the conclusion lands.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Review the lesson this question draws on and try again.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: choosing your approach for the format, structuring and designing for delivery, and correcting the common errors that weaken a talk. On their own they are three separate skills. This lesson brings them together into one preparation practice you can use every time.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run a flawless routine. The aim is to see these three moves as one practice rather than three separate skills, so that it carries into every presentation you give across your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect adapting to the format, structuring and designing for delivery, and correcting common errors into one preparation practice
analyse how the three work as one in a worked example of a student preparing for a presentation
apply the three together to prepare for a presentation in your own {{context}} study beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Preparing a presentation well is these three moves run as one practice. It is not three separate jobs but one routine you run each time you present: read the brief and the format, build a structure and visual aids that fit, then rehearse and correct the common errors before the day. The three skills from the earlier lessons are the parts of that one practice.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, the three moves are not three separate jobs but one run of preparation for a single talk. You read the brief to see what the format rewards, build a structure and visual aids that fit it, then rehearse and check the talk against the common errors before the day. Run as one practice, each move feeds the next, and the presentation you deliver is the one that was actually asked for.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a presentation coming up in your studies. How would you run the three moves on it: what does the brief reward, what structure fits, and which common error will you watch for?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: These three moves are strongest when you run them as one preparation practice, every time you present. Read the brief, build a structure and visual aids that fit, then rehearse and correct the common errors before the day. It is the practice, run each time, that makes your delivery reliable across your studies.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following sources.

_items.title: See pages 42 to 43 of Chapter 3 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 73 to 74 of Chapter 5 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The steps as one process
body: Preparing a presentation runs as one sequence you work through each time you present. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Read the brief
_items.body: Read the brief and criteria to see what the format is really testing.

_items.title: Build
_items.body: Build a structure and visual aids that fit that format.

_items.title: Rehearse
_items.body: Rehearse to time and check the talk against the common errors.

_items.title: Correct and deliver
_items.body: Correct what you find, deliver, and carry the lesson into your next presentation.

title: Worked example
body: Two students prepare the same assessed talk. Student A treats each stage on its own: slides first, a glance at the brief late on, and no rehearsal. Student B runs the three moves as one practice, reading the brief, building a fitting structure, then rehearsing and trimming the slides for the common errors. Student B's talk fits the task and lands, because the moves worked together.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to prepare for any presentation
body: Use these to run the three moves as one practice, rather than treating each presentation as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I read the brief and format before planning anything?
Does my structure fit this format, with visual aids that support it?
Have I rehearsed the talk to time?
Have I checked it against the common errors and corrected them?
Will I carry what I learn into my next presentation?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat these three moves as one preparation practice rather than three separate skills?
body: Why is it more useful to treat these three moves as one preparation practice rather than three separate skills?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat these three moves as one preparation practice rather than three separate skills?

_items.text: Because they work on the same presentation: the format you read shapes the structure you build, and the structure shapes the errors you watch for.
_items.feedback: Yes. Run as one practice, each move feeds the next, so the whole talk fits the task.

_items.text: Because a presentation only ever needs one of the three, so you can pick whichever is easiest.
_items.feedback: A good talk uses all three. They are parts of one practice, not a choice of one.

_items.text: Because treating them as one means you can skip reading the brief.
_items.feedback: Reading the brief is the first move. The practice includes it rather than skips it.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less thought than preparing at all.
_items.feedback: It is not about less thought. One routine spreads the thinking so it stays manageable.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three moves act on the same presentation, so running them as one practice makes the talk fit the task.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how reading the format, building the structure, and checking for errors work on the same talk.

displayTitle: A student reads the brief for a poster, designs a clear visual layout to fit it, rehearses the two-minute summary to time, and trims a crowded panel before the day. What does this show?
body: A student reads the brief for a poster, designs a clear visual layout to fit it, rehearses the two-minute summary to time, and trims a crowded panel before the day. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student reads the brief for a poster, designs a clear visual layout to fit it, rehearses the two-minute summary to time, and trims a crowded panel before the day. What does this show?

_items.text: The three moves working as one practice: adapting to the format, structuring and designing for it, and correcting the common errors.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reading the brief, designing to fit, and trimming for the errors are one connected run of preparation.

_items.text: That only the poster design mattered, and the brief and rehearsal made no difference.
_items.feedback: The design sat inside the whole practice. The brief and the rehearsal shaped it too.

_items.text: That the student prepared too much and should have done less.
_items.feedback: Each move did a job. Together they made the poster fit the task.

_items.text: That reading the brief is a separate task with nothing to do with the design.
_items.feedback: The brief shaped the design. That is why the moves belong to one practice.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student ran all three moves on the same poster, as one preparation practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the brief, the design and the rehearsal worked together on one poster.

displayTitle: You want to use this one preparation practice to present your {{context}} work better this term. Which plan best treats the three moves as one practice?
body: You want to use this one preparation practice to present your {{context}} work better this term. Which plan best treats the three moves as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this one preparation practice to present your your subject work better this term. Which plan best treats the three moves as one practice?

_items.text: For each presentation, read the brief and format, build a structure and visual aids to fit, then rehearse and check it against the common errors.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three moves together, every time, which is the practice working as it should.

_items.text: Always use the same slides and approach, whatever the brief asks for.
_items.feedback: That skips reading the format. The practice starts by adapting to what the brief rewards.

_items.text: Only check for errors on the presentations that went badly last time.
_items.feedback: Checking for errors is part of every run, not only after a talk goes wrong.

_items.text: Build the slides first, then read the brief if there is time left.
_items.feedback: The brief comes first. It shapes the structure and the slides, not the other way round.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading the brief, building a fitting structure, and checking for the common errors, every time, keeps the three moves as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan runs all three moves together on each presentation.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which description best fits preparing a presentation as one practice?
body: Which description best fits preparing a presentation as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which description best fits preparing a presentation as one practice?

_items.text: Running the three moves together on each talk: read the brief and format, build a fitting structure and visual aids, then check for the common errors.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Preparing the slides first and reading the brief only if there is time.
_items.feedback: The brief comes first and shapes the rest.

_items.text: Using the same approach for every format, whatever the brief asks.
_items.feedback: The practice begins by adapting to the format.

_items.text: Checking for errors only once the presentation is over.
_items.feedback: The common errors are fixed before the day, not after.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student reads the brief for a group talk, agrees a structure and handovers with the team, rehearses to time, and cuts two crowded slides before the day. Which parts of the practice has the student used?
body: A student reads the brief for a group talk, agrees a structure and handovers with the team, rehearses to time, and cuts two crowded slides before the day. Which parts of the practice has the student used?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student reads the brief for a group talk, agrees a structure and handovers with the team, rehearses to time, and cuts two crowded slides before the day. Which parts of the practice has the student used?

_items.text: Adapting to the format, structuring and designing for it, and correcting the common errors: the three moves as one practice.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Only the slide design; the brief and the rehearsal did not matter.
_items.feedback: The brief and the rehearsal shaped the talk too.

_items.text: Only the time limit; the structure and slides were irrelevant.
_items.feedback: The structure and slides were part of the same practice.

_items.text: None; preparing for a group talk uses none of the three moves.
_items.feedback: A group talk uses all three, run together.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
